food.text: The staple diet of ancient Egyptians consisted of bread and beer, supplemented with vegetables such as onions and garlic, and fruit such as dates and figs. Wine and meat were enjoyed by all on feast days, while the upper classes indulged more regularly.

Egyptian cuisine remained remarkably stable over time. The cuisine of modern Egypt still retains some striking similarities to the cuisine of the ancients, and fish, meat and fowl could be salted or dried, then cooked in stews or roasted on a grill.

Spices and herbs added flavor to Egyptian food, but the spices were expensive imports and so were confined to the tables of the wealthy. Meats were mostly preserved by salting, and dates and raisins could be dried for long-term storage.

Herodotus, a Greek historian of the 5th century BC, claimed that Egyptians abstained from eating female cows because they were sacred by association with Isis. Male oxen inspected and found clean and free of disease were sacrificed, and the remainder was eaten after being ritually burned. Male oxen that were ill or diseased, and not worthy of sacrifice, were ritually buried when they died, then dug up once the bones were clean and placed in a temple.

Ramesses IV saw issues with the provision of food rations to his workmen, similar to the situation under his father. Ramessesnakht, the High Priest of Amun, began to accompany state officials as they paid the rations, suggesting the Temple of Amun was partly responsible for the workmen's wages.

The chicken most likely arrived in Egypt around the 5th to 4th century BC, though no chicken bones have actually been found dating from before the Greco-Roman period. Other poultry possibly eaten included partridge, quail, pigeon, ducks and geese.

Pigs were among the most important food animals, alongside cattle, sheep and goats. They were previously thought to have been taboo to eat because the priests of Egypt referred pig to the evil god Seth. Excavations at the Giza workers' village uncovered evidence of massive slaughter of oxen, sheep and pigs, so large that researchers estimate the workforce building the Great Pyramid was fed beef every day.

Egyptians ate a dessert made from ground tiger nuts, the tuber of the chufa plant, mixed with honey. The tubers, stems and seeds of sedges such as papyrus, lotus and chufa were also eaten raw, boiled, roasted, or ground into flour.

Evidence is not conclusive on whether radishes, turnips and cabbage were available in Egypt before the Greco-Roman period. Celery had been introduced by the late New Kingdom, though it is uncertain whether it was used as food.
Greeks living in Egypt were not allowed the sacred sacrifice meat. According to Herodotus, the only part of the male oxen they could eat was the heads, which had been cut off and then cursed.

art.text: The ancient Egyptian language had no word for "art". Artworks served an essentially functional purpose bound up with religion and ideology, and to render a subject in art was to grant it permanence.

The Fayum mummy portraits are probably the most famous example of Egyptian art from the Roman period. They were naturalistic painted portraits on wooden boards, attached to the mummies of upper class people in Roman Egypt.

Kushite rulers in Nubia built pyramids as royal and elite tombs, a burial custom that lasted almost a thousand years, from 700 BC to 350 AD. The pyramids adapted Egyptian architecture from the New Kingdom, and they are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The Fayum portraits belong to the tradition of panel painting, one of the most highly regarded forms of art in the Classical world. They are the only large body of art from that tradition to have survived.

The earliest pyramids at El Kurru were constructed in 751 BC. The tradition of building royal Kushite pyramids is believed to have originated with King Piankhy, also called Piye, and it was continued by Shabaka, Shabataka and Tanwetamani.

When the Nubian capital moved from Napata to Meroe, rulers chose to be entombed there, and a new group of pyramids rose at Meroe from 270 BC. Construction lasted over 700 years, and the last Nubian pyramid, the last African pyramid, was built around 350 AD.

Some of Alexandria's underground catacombs were shared by the city's inhabitants to bury their dead. The Catacombs of Kom El Shoqafa were begun in the 1st century AD and continuously enlarged until the 3rd century. They mix classical and Egyptian decoration in a hybrid architectural style, and visitors can still see them today.
Piye's Victory Stela celebrates his campaigns between 728 and 716 BC. It was found in the Amun temple at Jebel Barkal, and it records his conquest of an Egypt fragmented into four kingdoms.

Although Kush shared many cultural affinities with Egypt, its people stayed distinct, and Egyptian art marked them out. Egyptian artists distinguished the people of Kush by their dress, their appearance, and even their method of transportation.

Egypt was the site of the earliest Christian monasteries, which became numerous by the end of the 4th century AD. Near Sohag, the Red Monastery, founded in the 4th century, and the White Monastery, from c. 440, are exceptional surviving examples of early Christian architecture.

At the Kharga Oasis, the El Bagawat necropolis holds tombs and small chapels from both pre-Christian and early Christian times. The Chapel of the Exodus, built around the early 4th century, is one of its oldest, and a nearby church possibly from the 5th century may be one of the oldest church remains in Egypt.

Arqamani, a Kushite ruler, constructed a small entrance hall to a temple built by Ptolemy IV and a temple at Philae. It has been suggested that Ptolemy V later defaced Arqamani's name on inscriptions at Philae.

war.text: In Year 8 of Ramesses III's reign, Egypt won the Battle of Djahy and the Battle of the Delta and repelled the invading Sea Peoples. An inscription says no land could resist their arms, and that in Amurru they "desolated its people and its land was like that which had never existed." The empire of the Hittites collapsed, never to rise again, and most of Egypt's trading partners were destroyed. Egypt was spared that ruin, though the struggle left the kingdom seriously crippled.

Egyptians called Nubia Ta-Seti, meaning "land of the bow", and archery was a primary feature of the armies of Kerma and Kush. Kushite arrows were often poison-tipped. Their volleys were so accurate that they decimated Persian ranks and sometimes targeted the faces and eyes of individual warriors. Later, Nubian archers showered Muslim invaders with arrows until the men were wounded and withdrew with gouged eyes, which earned the Nubians the name "the marksmen of the eye".

In Year 5 of his reign, Ramesses III defeated a Libyan invasion of Egypt by the Libu, Meshwesh and Seped people, who came through Marmarica. The same invaders had previously tried and failed to invade during the reign of Merneptah.

In 671 BC the Assyrian King Esarhaddon began the conquest of Egypt with a larger, better prepared force. Memphis was taken and Taharqa fled to Nubia, while his heir and other family members were taken to Nineveh as prisoners. Esarhaddon boasted that he "deported all Aethiopians from Egypt, leaving not one to pay homage to me."
The role of cavalry was extensive in Kush during the Meroitic period. It rested on innovation in chariotry, the use of war elephants and new cavalry tactics.

Ramesses III's mortuary temple at Medinet Habou shows a chaotic scene of boats and warriors entwined in battle in the Nile delta. It shows that the Sea Peoples were seaborne foes from different origins who launched a combined land-sea invasion.

Esarhaddon's 669 BC campaign to expel Taharqa was abandoned when Esarhaddon died at Harran on the way to Egypt. His successor Ashurbanipal took up the task, defeated Taharqa and drove his forces back into Nubia. Taharqa died in Napata soon after, in 664 BC.

Around 568 to 567 BC, in the fourth year of Amasis, Egypt was invaded by the Babylonians under Nebuchadnezzar II. Recent evidence suggests they were initially successful and gained a foothold, but Amasis' forces repelled them. This may have forced Nebuchadnezzar II to abandon his plans to conquer Egypt.

King Hakor of the Twenty-Ninth Dynasty, which ruled from Mendes between 398 and 380 BC, was able to defeat a Persian invasion during his reign. Egypt had been unable to shake off Persian rule until the end of the previous century.

Ramesses V died of smallpox in 1143 BC. The Turin Papyrus records that workmen of Set Maat had to keep stopping work on his tomb KV9 out of "fear of the enemy". This suggests Egypt could not defend itself against presumed Libyan raiding parties.

literature.text: Meroitic, the script of the Kingdom of Kush and Meroë, was built on Egyptian writing. It was used from the 2nd century BC until the early 5th century AD. Apart from Egyptian, it is the oldest written language in Africa.
In late antiquity, spoken Egyptian gained a new written form called Coptic. It used the Greek alphabet, with extra signs borrowed from Demotic for sounds that Greek letters did not represent.

Scribes stopped studying to read Egyptian hieroglyphs, and from roughly the 5th century CE the script was totally inscrutable. It stayed that way until decipherment in the early 19th century, which left Egypt's own recorded history inaccessible for centuries.
literature.source_title: Ancient Egypt in the Western imagination

literature.text: Towards the end of the New Kingdom, scribes began using the vernacular language for popular pieces. The Story of Wenamun tells of a noble who is robbed on his way to buy cedar from Lebanon, and of his struggle to return to Egypt.

During the Greco-Roman period, Egyptian literature was translated into other languages and Greco-Roman literature fused with native art into a new style of writing. Alexandria's center of learning also produced the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.

Greco-Roman poets came to Alexandria to find patrons and to use the resources of the Library of Alexandria. Callimachus of Libya and Theocritus of Syracuse were among them, and Nonnus of Panopolis, author of the epic poem Dionysiaca, was a notable Egyptian poet.

Manetho, an Egyptian historian known by his Greek name, worked during the reign of Ptolemy II. He wrote partly in response to Herodotus's Histories, and compiled the Aegyptiaca, the first comprehensive history of Egypt. He organized the rulers into the thirty-one dynasties still recognized today.

From about 700 BC, narrative stories and instructions were written in the demotic script and phase of Egyptian. The popular Instructions of Onchsheshonqy is one example, and personal and business documents were written in demotic too.

The Corpus Hermeticum is a dialogue between Hermes Trismegistus and a disciple. Most of it dates to the 1st to 4th century AD, in Roman Egypt. Its themes include summoning spirits, animating statues, astrology, alchemy and the purification of the soul.

Many demotic stories written in the Graeco-Roman period were set in earlier eras, when Egypt was an independent nation ruled by great pharaohs such as Ramesses II. Writers looked back to a proud past.

Coptic was not created by monks alone. Earlier experiments in writing Egyptian with Greek letters, bilingual scribal practice, priestly learning and Christian book production all contributed. Monastic communities then helped spread it by linking villages, towns, the Thebaid, Alexandria, pilgrims and scribal networks.

Diodorus Siculus records an inscription on the base of one of Ramesses II's sculptures: 'King of Kings am I, Osymandias.' It challenges anyone who would know how great he was to surpass one of his works. Percy Bysshe Shelley paraphrased it in his poem 'Ozymandias'.

Some Middle Kingdom genres, such as teachings and fictional tales, stayed popular in the New Kingdom. Prophetic texts, however, were not revived until the Ptolemaic period, which ran from the 4th century BC to the 1st century BC.

science.text: Alexandria in Lower Egypt became the centre of scientific activity across the Hellenistic world after Alexander the Great's conquests. There the native Egyptian astronomy tradition merged with Greek and Babylonian astronomy.

Roman Egypt produced Claudius Ptolemy (90-168 CE), called the greatest astronomer of his era. He came from the Thebaid region of Upper Egypt and worked at Alexandria. His works on astronomy became the most influential books in the history of Western astronomy.

Egyptian geometry grew out of surveying, which was needed to preserve the layout and ownership of fertile farmland flooded each year by the Nile. Rules of thumb such as the 3,4,5 right triangle helped represent rectilinear structures.
The Lighthouse of Alexandria was designed by Sostratus of Cnidus and built between 285 and 247 BC on the island of Pharos. It was renowned in its time, and knowledge of it was never lost.

In Alexandria, medical officials were allowed to cut open and examine human corpses to learn how the body worked, beginning with Ptolemy I Soter. An important school of medicine formed there from the late 4th century to the 2nd century BC.
Alexandria was a busy port for ships trading goods made in or imported into Egypt. A giant cantilevered hoist lifted cargo to and from the ships.
The Greek astronomer Eratosthenes (c. 276-195 BCE) was the greatest Alexandrian astronomer of the Ptolemaic era. He calculated the size of the Earth, providing an estimate for its circumference.
Recent scholarship suggests the water wheel originated in Ptolemaic Egypt, appearing by the 3rd century BC. The oldest archaeological evidence is a Sakia at Faiyum dating to the 3rd century BC.
Iron technology reached Kush through the Assyrians after their conquest of Egypt. It allowed Nubia to manufacture iron weapons such as swords, spears and armor.

Herophilos (335-280 BC) and Erasistratus (c. 304 - c. 250 BC) made the first use of human bodies for anatomical research. They gained permission to perform live dissections, or vivisections, on condemned criminals in Alexandria under the Ptolemaic dynasty, cutting open living people who had been sentenced to death.
Ptolemy wrote the Almagest, the Planetary Hypotheses and the Tetrabiblos. He also produced the Handy Tables and the Canobic Inscription, along with other works unrelated to astronomy.
A 2nd-century BC papyrus from Faiyum mentions a water wheel used for irrigation. A fresco of the same century from Alexandria depicts a compartmented Sakia.

Herodotus reported that Necho II sent out an expedition of Phoenicians, which reputedly sailed in three years from the Red Sea around Africa to the mouth of the Nile. It took place at some point between 610 and before 594 BC, though some Egyptologists doubt a pharaoh would authorize it.

Callixenus of Rhodes wrote of a Sakia used in Ptolemaic Egypt during the reign of Ptolemy IV in the late 3rd century BC. According to John Peter Oleson, the compartmented wheel and the hydraulic noria may have been invented in Egypt by the 4th century BC.

politics.text: Egypt was a wealthy imperial province of the Roman Empire, supplying grain and hosting the major city of Alexandria. Its population primarily spoke Greek in major cities and Coptic Egyptian in rural areas.

The Twenty-fifth Dynasty was a line of pharaohs from the Kingdom of Kush, in present-day northern Sudan. They reigned over part or all of Egypt from 744 to 656 BC. Their reunification of Lower Egypt, Upper Egypt, and Kush created the largest Egyptian empire since the New Kingdom.

Ptolemy, a trusted general of Alexander the Great, was appointed satrap of Egypt and ruled from 323 BC. In 305 BC he took the title of basileus and pharaoh as Ptolemy I Soter, meaning Saviour. He founded the Ptolemaic dynasty, which ruled Egypt for nearly 300 years.

In 525 BC the Persian Empire, led by Cambyses II, began its conquest of Egypt and defeated the pharaoh Psamtik III at the Battle of Pelusium. Cambyses II took the formal title of pharaoh but ruled Egypt from Iran, leaving the country under the control of a satrap.

The Assyrians left Egypt in the hands of vassals known as the Saite kings of the Twenty-Sixth Dynasty. By 653 BC the Saite king Psamtik I was able to oust the Assyrians with the help of Greek mercenaries. These mercenaries were recruited to form Egypt's first navy.

Egypt regained independence in 402 BC, ending its first period of Persian rule, and native dynasties followed. The Thirtieth Dynasty proved to be the last native royal house of ancient Egypt, ending with the kingship of Nectanebo II.

The Kushite king Taharqa and his army defeated the Assyrians outright in 674 BC, according to Babylonian records. Yet in 671 BC Esarhaddon defeated Taharqa in Egypt, conquered Northern Egypt, captured Memphis, imposed tribute, and withdrew. Taharqa reoccupied Memphis and the Delta in 669 BC, but Esarhaddon again led his army to Egypt, and on his death the command passed to Ashurbanipal, whose Assyrians advanced as far south as Thebes. Taharqa retreated to Nubia, where he died in 664 BC.

In Year 8 of Ramesses III's reign, the Twentieth Dynasty defeated the invading Sea Peoples in the Battle of Djahy and the Battle of the Delta. Other lands were not so lucky. An inscription says the Sea Peoples "desolated" the people of Amurru until its land "was like that which had never existed", and the empire of the Hittites collapsed, never to rise again. Egypt's many new temples displayed its power, but they also show the political ascendancy of the priesthood over the pharaoh.

Ptolemy successfully defended Egypt against an invasion by Perdiccas in 321 BC. He then consolidated his position in Egypt and the surrounding areas during the Wars of the Diadochi, which ran from 322 to 301 BC.

After Queen Twosret, the last pharaoh of the 19th Dynasty, died, Egypt entered a civil war, as attested by the Elephantine stela built by Setnakhte. Her fate is uncertain, since she may have died peacefully or been overthrown. The war ended when Setnakhte took the throne and founded the 20th Dynasty.

In 701 BC, Taharqa and his army aided Judah and King Hezekiah in withstanding a siege by King Sennacherib of Assyria. Historians disagree over why the Assyrians withdrew without taking Jerusalem. Some evidence, such as Khor paying tribute to Amun of Karnak, argues against the view that Sennacherib became overlord of Khor.

Ramesses V reigned for no more than 4 years and died of smallpox in 1143 BC. The Turin Papyrus says workmen on his KV9 tomb had to stop periodically out of "fear of the enemy". This suggests growing instability and an inability to defend Egypt from presumed Libyan raiding parties.

philosophy.text: A manuscript called "The Immortality of Writers", or "Be a Writer", dates to about 1200 BC and is attributed to the writer Irsesh. It states: "Man perishes; his corpse turns to dust; all his relatives return to the earth." Only writings make a man remembered in the mouth of the reader, and a book is more effective than a well-built house or a tomb-chapel. Dag Herbjørnsrud, writing for the American Philosophical Association, calls it a "remarkable example of classical Egyptian philosophy."

Several ancient Greek philosophers regarded Egypt as a place of wisdom. Isocrates says in Busiris that the Egyptians introduced philosophy's training for the soul, and that Greek writers traveled there to seek knowledge. He names Pythagoras of Samos as one who brought all philosophy to the Greeks.

Christianity's strict monotheism was in stark opposition to the freeform syncretism of paganism, and local Christians engaged in campaigns of proselytism and iconoclasm that eroded traditional Egyptian religion. The article says priests, bishops, and monks rampaged through the countryside, intent on "eradicating demons". Egypt had become an early centre of Christianity even before the Edict of Milan in AD 313, and Alexandria was home to influential writers such as Origen and Clement of Alexandria.

In Plato's Phaedrus, the Egyptian Thoth is said to have invented numbers and arithmetic. Most important of all, he is credited with inventing letters. Plato thus presents the Egyptian god as the source of key tools of learning.

After Alexander the Great's conquest and the rise of the Ptolemaic dynasty, Greeks in Egypt became the ruling elite. Greek philosophers and scholars in Alexandria confronted a civilization far older than their own. The encounter inspired the idea of Egypt as an ancient and enduring source of religious wisdom.
philosophy.source_title: Ancient Egypt in the Western imagination

philosophy.text: Under the Ptolemaic dynasty (305 to 30 BC), the Greek ruling class identified Egyptian deities with their own. From this blending emerged Serapis, a god who combined Osiris and Apis with characteristics of Greek deities and became very popular among the Greek population. Even so, the two belief systems mostly stayed separate.
The Desert Fathers were early Christian hermits and ascetics who lived mainly in the Wadi El Natrun, then known as Skete, in Roman Egypt. They began to settle there around the third century.
philosophy.source_title: Ancient Egypt in the Western imagination

philosophy.text: In Plato's Timaeus, Socrates quotes Egyptian wise men speaking to the law-giver Solon, who traveled to Egypt to learn. They tell him, "O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children."
Aristotle attests to Egypt being the original land of wisdom. He states in Politics that "Egyptians are reputed to be the oldest of nations, but they have always had laws and a political system."

The Egyptian admiral Wedjahor-Resne recorded that Cambyses respected Egyptian religious customs. When Cambyses placed troops near the Temple of Neith at Sais, Wedjahor-Resne persuaded him to move them, because their presence might have been viewed as sacrilegious by the gods.
Even at the end of the 5th century, the Neo-Platonist philosopher Heraescus was buried according to pagan rites. He was possibly the uncle and father-in-law of Horapollo.

culture.text: The Library of Alexandria was once the largest in the world. It is usually assumed to have been founded at the beginning of the 3rd century BC under Ptolemy II, and at its peak it is estimated to have stored 400,000 to 700,000 scrolls.

Egyptians called Nubia Ta-Seti, meaning "land of the bow." Nubia had a strong relationship with archery throughout antiquity, and bows and arrows accompanied male burials of all ages. Kushite arrows were often poison-tipped, and the Nobadians shot barbed and possibly poisoned arrows about 50 cm long.

The cult of the goddess Isis became popular in the Roman Empire, as obelisks and other relics were transported back to Rome. The Romans also imported building materials from Egypt to build Egyptian-style structures, and came to view Egypt as a place of mystery.

Herodotus wrote in his Histories, around 440 BC, that the only deities worshipped at the Aethiopian capital of Meroë were Zeus (Amun) and Dionysus (Osiris). He described Aethiopia as all the inhabited land south of Egypt, beginning at Elephantine.

The Ptolemies adopted pharaonic traditions to legitimise their rule. They appeared on monuments in Egyptian style and took part in local religious life, even though Alexandria remained a centre of Greek culture and trade.

Egyptian civilization strongly influenced the Kingdom of Kush and Meroë, which adopted Egyptian religious and architectural norms. Hundreds of pyramids, 6 to 30 meters high, were built in Egypt and Sudan, and Egyptian writing became the basis of the Meroitic script.

Alexandria was home to influential Christian writers such as Origen and Clement of Alexandria, and its church credits its founding to Mark the Evangelist, c. AD 42. Under Pope Demetrius I, a bishop from AD 189 to 231, Christianity spread up the Nile. Persecution followed: Septimius Severus in AD 202 dissolved the Catechetical School of Alexandria and forbade conversion, and in AD 303 Diocletian ordered all churches destroyed, sacred books burned, and all Christians who were not officials enslaved. Many Egyptian Christians survived because they were sent instead to work in quarries and mines as penal labour.

Under the Persians, Egyptian religion did not suffer. The Egyptian admiral Wedjahor-Resne recorded that Cambyses respected religious customs, and when Cambyses placed troops near the Temple of Neith at Sais, Wedjahor-Resne convinced him to move them, since their presence might have been seen as sacrilegious.

Egyptian Christians of the late Roman Empire abhorred the religion and culture of ancient Egypt. General Christian opposition to paganism targeted Greco-Roman deities and temples, and people too (the article points to Hypatia and the Serapeum of Alexandria). Egyptian Christianity developed a distinct antagonism toward native Egyptian religious practices still active in some regions, and toward the whole of Egypt's pre-Christian culture and history. Temples to Isis, Horus and Thoth were denounced as demonic, and anti-paganism policies of the early Byzantine Empire caused the defacement, repurposing or destruction of artwork, monuments and temples.
culture.source_title: Ancient Egypt in the Western imagination

culture.text: The name Nubia is thought to derive from nub, the Egyptian word for gold. It is believed that Nubians were the first people along the Nile to mine gold, later introducing it to the Egyptians.

Around 700 BC the Nubians adopted the Egyptian hieroglyphic system. Later, after the collapse of Kush and the closure of the last Ancient Egyptian temple by Emperor Justinian I, they gradually converted to Christianity.
